whatItFakes: A bill drafted from the seat phases in an amount only by dated steps the sponsor names (one section per step). The ruling's other form, an amount that rises by a percent a year, cannot be drafted: the seat takes no rate and no span.
why: The owner ruled that bills phase in by dated steps or a percent a year (DECISION-REGISTER, Sept 12 travel clarification, item 1); pool item gov-m3-01-phase-in-by-dated-steps built the dated steps first, and how a yearly percent is written into law (a step per year, or one indexed row the laws engine raises each year) is not built.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: seatAct takes a percent a year and the years it runs; the steps are drafted as dated sections of the one bill a year apart, each the law in force raised by the percent, through the same enact path (or one indexed law row the laws engine raises each year on its calendar), with no number typed.
resolvedBy: stand-in triage T9 (owner, Nov 10: too in depth)

whatItFakes: A budget-line section that names its own effective date (provisionFor with an effectiveDate) is amended into the budget the day the bill becomes law: amendBudget takes no date, so every step of a budget phase-in would land at once; seatAct refuses phase-in steps on a budget line for that reason.
why: enact reads each law section's date through enactLaw and the laws engine's calendar, but a budget line has no dated amendment in the budgets engine; found building pool item gov-m3-01-phase-in-by-dated-steps, whose test phases in a wage floor instead.
replacement: The budgets engine amends a line on the section's date: enact schedules the dated budget section on the calendar (as enactLaw does a dated law row) and amendBudget applies it to the fiscal year that date falls in, so lawmakers and the budget screen read each step when it lands; seatAct then takes phase-in steps on a budget line, as it does on a law amount.

whatItFakes: Cosponsors are recorded only for the bill the played official sponsors; other members' bills carry none.
why: Reading every member's position on every drafted bill in a 435-member House each day would slow a country's year past the speed bar; a member's own bill is the one a player reads.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Record cosponsors for every full person's bill from the same rule, once the position read is cheap enough, and fold the counted members' signatures as a count.
resolvedBy: stand-in triage T9 (owner, Nov 10: too in depth)

whatItFakes: A study committee's size (studyMembers = 5) and term (studyTermDays = 180) are TUNABLE placeholders, and its members are the sponsor and the opponents nearest to changing their vote. Real interim and study committees are formed by constitution, statute or chamber rule, may draw from one or both chambers and sometimes include outsiders (NCSL, from a search snippet only); no outsiders sit here, and no rule of any body's decides when it forms one.
why: The NCSL pages on interim and study committees (ncsl.org) and a Montana Legislative Council memo could not be fetched in this session (hosts outside the network allowlist), so no sourced size, term or formation rule was read. The formation cause is the game's own: a narrow floor loss whose closest opponents are less sure than its backers.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Per-body formation rules, sizes and terms read from NCSL and each legislature's rules (and mayoral or county task force practice), with outside members drawn from residents by their records.
resolvedBy: stand-in triage T9 (owner, Nov 10: too in depth)
